lead.headline: Grieve capsule sealed beneath the Flushing library's reading room floor
lead.deck: 38 records and an empty sleeve numbered 23 in a copper box; Mr. Abbot present nine minutes; to be opened June 15, 1978
lead.body: Mrs. Ottoline Grieve sealed 38 records for 1978 into a copper box at the Flushing Free Library yesterday, the solder being applied at 11:42 a.m., the library states. The box holds the thirteen mothers' records and an empty sleeve numbered 23 in Mrs. Grieve's hand. It was lowered beneath the reading room floor at noon. Mr. Cyril Abbot of the Phonautograph Society was present for nine minutes and left before the solder was applied. The library's house system recorded the sealing. That record is not in the box.

columns.headline: Receiver to sell 61,000 Hollander valves in lots of 600 from 9 a.m. tomorrow
columns.body: Mr. Reuben Tate, receiver of the Hollander Valve & Supply Co., will sell the stock of the Jamaica Avenue warehouse in lots of 600 from 9 a.m. tomorrow, cash only, his office states. About 640 grocers hold tickets. Valves held at 90 cents the six yesterday.

columns.headline: Justice Lowry to hear counsel on the primary counts at 10 a.m. tomorrow
columns.body: Justice Arthur Lowry will hear counsel for Alderman John Feeney and Former Commissioner Augustin Dolan at Long Island City at 10 a.m. tomorrow on the two counts of the June 4 primary. The sealed records of 386 polling places will be brought from the Board at 7 a.m.

columns.headline: Phonautograph Society to record the dawn at Alley Pond on Friday
columns.body: The Phonautograph Society of Queens will record the dawn chorus at Alley Pond on Friday, the longest day of the year, from 4:50 a.m., sunrise being at 5:25 a.m., Mr. Cyril Abbot states. The record is intended for 1978. Members are asked to be silent.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: WORS 1610 was not heard last night, the thirty-ninth night since May 7, the Radio Division states.

speaker.ear: Fair. High 80. Sunday. The capsule's under the floor. Mind the gap.

lead.headline: The early bird gets the record: Abbot's men to catch the dawn at Alley Pond
lead.deck: Fourteen machines in the reeds by ten to five on Friday, the longest day; members forbidden to cough; Mrs. Grieve not invited, but may attend, which is how Mr. Abbot puts it
lead.body: On Friday, the longest day of the year, Mr. Abbot and the Phonautograph Society will be in the reeds at Alley Pond by ten to five in the morning with fourteen machines, to record the dawn for 1978. Members may not speak, cough or swat. Mr. Abbot asks the dairies of Douglaston to hold their wagons until six. The dairies have asked who will milk the cows. Mrs. Grieve is not invited but may attend, which is exactly the phrase she used about him. The birds have not been told.

columns.headline: Ask the Operator: 'Will the judge pick up the wire or the pencil?'
columns.body: Sir, Justice Lowry hears both counts tomorrow at ten, and the operator would not presume. She will say that in her experience the man who writes things down usually wins the argument, and the man who recorded it usually wins the next one.

columns.headline: Where's WORS? Thirty-nine nights, and the night clerk takes up knitting
columns.body: Thirty-nine nights since WORS last came on sixteen-ten. Mr. Pike's shore men sit from half past ten to midnight regardless. The night clerk has finished one sock and begun another. Our office boy has oiled pin ninety-seven against the rust, in case.

columns.headline: The Listening Lady: a copper box, a closed door, and one empty sleeve
columns.body: Darlings, the Listening Lady was at the Flushing library for the sealing and has nothing to report, which is unheard of. Mr. Abbot stood at the back. Mrs. Grieve stood at the front. The sleeve stood empty between them. The solder set at eleven forty-two.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: The library's own machine recorded the sealing. It is not in the box. It is in a drawer. We asked.

lead.headline: Justice Lowry hears counsel today on the two counts of the Queens primary
lead.deck: Sealed polling-place records brought under guard from the Board at 7 a.m.; the wire gives Feeney 211, the paper Dolan 38; 249 votes differ in 23 districts
lead.body: Justice Arthur Lowry of the Supreme Court will hear counsel at Long Island City at 10 a.m. today on the two counts of the June 4 Democratic primary for Borough President, the wire giving Alderman John Feeney a margin of 211 and the paper giving Former Commissioner Augustin Dolan a margin of 38. The house records of 386 polling places will be brought from the Board of Elections under guard at 7 a.m. The counts differ by 249 votes in 23 districts. Neither candidate will address the court.

columns.headline: Athletics lead by eight games; Mr. Ruth hits his fourteenth home run
columns.body: The Athletics won twice from St. Louis and lead the American League by eight games. The Yankees split two with Chicago at the Stadium, Mr. Ruth hitting his fourteenth home run of the season in yesterday's second inning. Brooklyn lost twice to Boston.

columns.headline: Hollander valve sale opens at 9 a.m. today; about 640 grocers hold tickets
columns.body: Mr. Reuben Tate, receiver of the Hollander Valve & Supply Co., opens the sale of 61,000 valves at the Jamaica Avenue warehouse at 9 a.m. today in lots of 600. The Jamaica precinct will send four patrolmen. Long-life valves will be sold separately.

columns.headline: Mr. Pruett's trial in Special Sessions opens tomorrow at 10 a.m.
columns.body: Mr. Gideon Pruett of Whitney Avenue, Elmhurst, will be tried in Special Sessions at Long Island City at 10 a.m. tomorrow, Justice Cornelius Hagan presiding, on the first charge under section 14 of the Listening Act. Mrs. Agnes Dorr will give evidence for the State.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: WORS 1610 was not heard last night, the fortieth night since May 7, the Radio Division states.

speaker.ear: Fair. High 83. Monday. Valves by the gross. Bring a barrow.

lead.headline: Six hundred grocers queue for Hollander's valves, and the bidding warms up
lead.deck: Sixty-one thousand tubes in lots of six hundred; the first lot goes at four dollars and ten cents the hundred; a Corona widow buys three lots and borrows a horse to carry them
lead.body: The Hollander warehouse on Jamaica Avenue opened at nine this morning and six hundred and forty grocers came in at once, four patrolmen holding the door. Mr. Tate, the receiver, sold the first lot of six hundred valves at four dollars and ten cents the hundred, which is about a quarter the six. By four o'clock the warehouse was empty except for the long-life grade and Mr. Hollander, who watched from the stairs. A Corona widow bought three lots and borrowed a coal horse to carry them home.

columns.headline: Lowry hears both sides of the line, and puts the count on hold till Thursday
columns.body: Justice Lowry heard counsel for four hours today and had three of the twenty-three disputed polling places played aloud in court. They sounded like polling places. He reserved judgment till Thursday. Duke sat outside on the steps, being barred, and was given water by a bailiff.

columns.headline: Babe connects for fourteen, and Philadelphia still won't return the call
columns.body: The Babe hit his fourteenth of the year yesterday against Chicago, a long one to right that a Bronx subscriber reported to the Exchange as thunder. The Yankees split the pair. Philadelphia won two more and is eight games clear. Mr. Huggins has stopped saying it is June.

columns.headline: Ask the Operator: 'Who is right, my clock or the pips?'
columns.body: Sir, the pips. The clock on your landing is only somebody's opinion. Station time comes down every evening at eight. Stand in your lobby with a set and you will soon know how long your landlord has been lying to you. Some lobbies run four minutes fast, and the tenants have never been late for anything.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Mr. Hollander was the last man out of the warehouse. He took one valve in his pocket. Nobody stopped him.

lead.headline: Justice Lowry reserves decision on the primary after four hours of argument
lead.deck: Three disputed polling places' records played in court; Mr. Dolan's counsel: 'the voter does not speak'; Alderman Feeney's counsel: 'the room does'; decision Thursday at 10 a.m.
lead.body: Justice Arthur Lowry heard counsel on the two counts of the June 4 primary for four hours at Long Island City yesterday and reserved decision until 10 a.m. Thursday. At his direction the records of three of the 23 disputed polling places were played in court, among them P.S. 84, Astoria. Mr. Dolan's counsel, Mr. Felix Arbogast, argued that 'the voter does not speak; he marks.' Alderman Feeney's counsel, Mr. Oren Stahl, replied, according to the court's record, that 'the room speaks for him.'

columns.headline: Receiver sells 58,200 Hollander valves in one day; retail price at 80 cents
columns.body: Mr. Reuben Tate, receiver of the Hollander Valve & Supply Co., sold 97 lots, 58,200 valves, at the Jamaica Avenue warehouse yesterday at prices from 3.80 to 4.10 dollars the hundred. Valves were quoted at retail at 80 cents the six by 5 p.m.

columns.headline: Mr. Pruett on trial today; the Whitney Avenue system to be played to the court
columns.body: Mr. Gideon Pruett will be tried in Special Sessions at 10 a.m. today before Justices Hagan, Melvin and Kopf. The State will play four minutes of the record of March 9 from his house system, the District Attorney states. Mrs. Agnes Dorr and two former tenants will testify.

columns.headline: Weather Bureau forecasts 90 degrees by Thursday; ice companies add wagons
columns.body: The Weather Bureau forecasts temperatures of 90 degrees or more in the city by Thursday. The Astoria Lake, Jamaica Pond and Flushing Bay ice companies will put six more wagons on the road from today, Mr. Gustave Pohl states, at the summer price of 55 cents.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: WORS 1610 was not heard last night, the forty-first night since May 7, the Radio Division states.

speaker.ear: Warm. High 86. Tuesday. Pruett's day in court. His walls testify.

lead.headline: Mrs. Dorr's kitchen takes the stand, and Pruett can't hang up on it
lead.deck: Four minutes of the night of March 9 played to three justices; Mrs. Dorr knows her own voice, her kettle and her curtain; the court finds at ten past five
lead.body: At eleven this morning Special Sessions played Mrs. Agnes Dorr's kitchen on the night of the fire, four minutes from Mr. Pruett's cellar, and then asked Mrs. Dorr whether it was her kitchen. She said it was. She knew the kettle. She knew her own voice saying 'the curtain, the curtain.' Then she said, 'I heard it once before, in the insurance man's office, when he told me no.' Mr. Pruett's counsel asked her no questions. At ten past five the court found Mr. Pruett guilty.

columns.headline: Lowry holds the line till Thursday, and both camps stay on the wire
columns.body: Justice Lowry reserved judgment yesterday after hearing three polling places played aloud in court. Mr. Dolan's man said a voter marks and does not speak. Mr. Feeney's man said the room speaks for him. The room, being sealed, declined to comment. Thursday at ten.

columns.headline: Heat on the line by Thursday, and the ice men put six more horses out
columns.body: The Weather Bureau promises ninety by Thursday. The ice companies have put six more wagons on the road, which makes twenty-eight, and Duchess will do the Steinway route twice a day in her hat. The Bureau advises shade. Queens has none to spare.

columns.headline: Pun Derby: week three's early leader, and the dead line comes in on time
columns.body: Leading after two days: Mrs. Ida Kranz of Maspeth, an undertaker's wife. 'I rang the cemetery and the operator couldn't put me through. It was a dead line.' Mr. Kehoe's horse has sent a card reading only 'Neigh.' The judges decline to hear it.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Mr. Pruett fined two hundred and fifty dollars. He paid at the window, in silver, from a cellar tin.

lead.headline: Mr. Pruett convicted under section 14 of the Listening Act; fined 250 dollars
lead.deck: First conviction under the Act; Justice Hagan orders the Whitney Avenue system licensed within 30 days or disconnected; Mrs. Dorr's evidence heard at 11:06 a.m.
lead.body: Mr. Gideon Pruett of Whitney Avenue, Elmhurst, was convicted in Special Sessions yesterday of selling a room's record without a licence, the first conviction under section 14 of the Listening Act, and fined 250 dollars, Justice Cornelius Hagan presiding. The court ordered his house system licensed within 30 days or disconnected. Mrs. Agnes Dorr, whose kitchen record was sold for 15 dollars, testified at 11:06 a.m. that she had 'heard it once before, in the adjuster's office, when he told me no.'

columns.headline: Atlas Casualty Co. to reconsider Mrs. Dorr's claim for the fire of March 9
columns.body: The Atlas Casualty Co. states that it will reconsider the claim of Mrs. Agnes Dorr for the kitchen fire of March 9 at Whitney Avenue, Elmhurst, 'without reference to any record,' following Mr. Pruett's conviction. Mr. Leon Harsch, adjuster, has been given leave.

columns.headline: Dr. Strand to sail for Wales on the Cedric on July 3; purpose not stated
columns.body: Dr. Matthias Strand of Union Seminary will sail for Liverpool on the Cedric on July 3 and spend the summer in Wales, the seminary states. Dr. Strand states that the visit is 'private,' and declines to say whether it concerns the piece he sang on June 2.

columns.headline: Senate vault's record of March 27 unclaimed in its thirteenth week
columns.body: Mr. Lyman Pratt, Clerk of the Senate, states that the committee room's record of March 27, containing the word 'resent,' remains in the vault at Albany, unclaimed, in its thirteenth week. Senator Rufus Keel has written about it a fourth time.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: WORS 1610 was not heard last night, the forty-second night since May 7, the Radio Division states.

speaker.ear: Hot. High 89. Wednesday. Ninety tomorrow. The ice man's whistling.

lead.headline: Queens moves out to the fire escape, and the whole block's on the party line
lead.deck: Mattresses on the tar roofs of Sunnyside and the fire escapes of Long Island City; every neighbour's conversation in every neighbour's ear, no machine required
lead.body: It was eighty-nine at four this afternoon and the Bureau promises ninety tomorrow, so last night Queens dragged its mattresses out onto the fire escapes and the tar roofs and lay there in rows, talking. Nobody needed a house system to hear the neighbours. A Sunnyside man heard his upstairs neighbour's whole opinion of him, and answered it. A Long Island City baby was sung to by three floors at once. Our man slept on the Speaker's own roof and heard the Hum, the elevated and his editor snoring.

columns.headline: Pruett pays up, and his cellar gets thirty days to licence or disconnect
columns.body: Mr. Pruett paid two hundred and fifty dollars in silver for selling Mrs. Dorr's kitchen for fifteen, which is the worst trade in Elmhurst this year. He has thirty days to licence his cellar or disconnect it. The insurance company now wants another look at Mrs. Dorr's claim.

columns.headline: Strand ships out for Wales, and the word stays on hold till September
columns.body: Dr. Strand sails on the Cedric on the third of July to spend the summer in Wales. He says it is private. We say a man who crosses the Atlantic for one word should at least tell us what it rhymes with. He declined, politely, in English.

columns.headline: The Listening Lady: the roofs of Sunnyside, after dark
columns.body: Darlings, the Listening Lady spent last night on a Sunnyside roof, as society now does, and can report one proposal, two quarrels and a man reciting the Polish alphabet to himself. The proposal was accepted on the third roof down. Congratulations, all of you.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: The vault in Albany still has 'resent.' Senator Keel has written a fourth time. He now signs it 'Yours, again.'

lead.headline: Temperature reaches 91 at 3:40 p.m.; four prostrations; 410,000 at Rockaway
lead.deck: Hottest day of the year; the Exchange logs 2,206 night calls, most asking that neighbours on the roofs be quieted; Board of Health advises against sleeping on the elevated's embankments
lead.body: The temperature reached 91 degrees at 3:40 p.m. yesterday at the Weather Bureau's station, the year's highest, and four persons were overcome in Queens, the police state. About 410,000 persons visited Rockaway Beach. The Queens Exchange logged 2,206 calls between 10 p.m. and 2 a.m., about twice the June figure, the greater part from subscribers asking that neighbours sleeping on roofs and fire escapes 'be asked to be quiet.' The Board of Health advises against sleeping on the elevated's embankments.

columns.headline: Justice Lowry to give his decision on the primary at 10 a.m. today
columns.body: Justice Arthur Lowry will give his decision on the two counts of the June 4 Democratic primary for Borough President at 10 a.m. today at Long Island City, the clerk states. Alderman John Feeney and Former Commissioner Augustin Dolan will attend. Duke will not be admitted.

columns.headline: Light company states July bills will show the half cent as 'Commission credit'
columns.body: Queens Light & Power states that the July bills of about 21,000 subscribers in Astoria and Steinway will show the half cent collected since May 1 as a line reading 'Commission credit,' averaging 19 cents. Alderman Feeney asks that it read 'Refund.'

columns.headline: Phonautograph Society to set 14 machines at Alley Pond at 4:50 a.m. tomorrow
columns.body: Mr. Cyril Abbot states that 31 members of the Phonautograph Society will set 14 machines in the reeds at Alley Pond at 4:50 a.m. tomorrow, sunrise being at 5:25 a.m., and record until 6:15. The Douglaston dairies have agreed to hold their wagons.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: WORS 1610 was not heard last night, the forty-third night since May 7, the Radio Division states.

speaker.ear: Hot. High 91. Thursday. The pencil wins. The wire sulks.

lead.headline: Lowry picks the pencil, and Dolan takes the nomination by a lead
lead.deck: Justice Lowry: the vote is the mark, and the room is only a witness; thirty-eight for Dolan; Feeney says 'the pencil has it' and shakes hands, Duke abstaining
lead.body: At ten this morning Justice Lowry ruled that a vote is a mark made with a pencil, and that a polling place's machine is a witness to the room the mark was made in, which is not the same thing. So the paper count stands, and Mr. Dolan is the Democrat by thirty-eight. Alderman Feeney stood up, said 'The pencil has it,' and shook Mr. Dolan's hand on the court steps. Duke did not shake. Mr. Senn logged 'two hands, one dog, ninety-one in the shade.'

columns.headline: Ninety-one, and the whole borough rings the operator to complain about itself
columns.body: The Exchange took twenty-two hundred calls last night between ten and two, twice the usual, mostly people on roofs asking the operator to tell the people on the next roof to hush. The operator cannot reach a roof. She advised a hat and patience.

columns.headline: Light company credits the half cent, and Feeney wants the line reworded
columns.body: Queens Light & Power will print the half cent on the July bill as 'Commission credit.' Alderman Feeney, having lost a primary this morning, found time to ask that it say 'Refund.' The company says a credit is not a refund. Nineteen cents, whatever it is called.

columns.headline: Ask the Operator: 'Can I ring the birds before Friday?'
columns.body: Madam, the birds of Alley Pond are not on the exchange, and the operator has tried. Mr. Abbot's society will be in the reeds at ten to five tomorrow. If you wish to be on the record, sing quietly. If you are a rooster, please hold.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: The twenty-three disputed polling places stay sealed. Justice Lowry has sent them to Mr. Crane 'as a licensing matter.'

record.ear: Hot. High 90. Low 72. Sunrise 5:25 a.m. The longest day.

lead.headline: Justice Lowry rules the paper count the count; Mr. Dolan nominated by 38
lead.deck: 'The vote is the mark; the room is a witness to it'; the 23 disputed districts' records referred to the Listening Act office; Alderman Feeney states he will not appeal
lead.body: Justice Arthur Lowry ruled at Long Island City yesterday that the paper count of the June 4 Democratic primary is the count, and that Former Commissioner Augustin Dolan is nominated for Borough President by 38 votes. 'The vote is the mark,' the Justice stated. 'The room is a witness to it, and a witness is not the vote.' The records of the 23 disputed districts were referred to Mr. Hollis Crane's office. Alderman John Feeney states that he will not appeal.

columns.headline: Appellate Division to rise for the summer on June 28; Riverhead seal undecided
columns.body: The Appellate Division will rise for the summer on June 28, the clerk states, with the appeal of Mr. Francis Gorman against the seal on 11 seconds of the Riverhead record undecided. Mr. Gorman attended yesterday, his thirty-fifth sitting, and noted the date.

columns.headline: Board of Elections states it will count November's ballots on paper first
columns.body: Chairman Delaney states that the Board of Elections will count the November ballots in Queens on paper first and by wire after, reversing the order used since last November, following Justice Lowry's decision. The clerks 'will be retrained again,' he states.

columns.headline: Third day of heat; Board of Health opens 14 school playgrounds overnight
columns.body: The Board of Health will open 14 school playgrounds in Queens as sleeping grounds from 9 p.m. tonight, with water and a patrolman at each, the temperature having stood above 88 for three days. Ice is quoted at 55 cents the hundredweight, unchanged.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: WORS 1610 was not heard last night, the forty-fourth night since May 7, the Radio Division states.

speaker.ear: Hot. High 90. Friday. The longest day. Twelve Fridays.

lead.headline: Alley Pond's dawn chorus goes on the record, and the band needs no conductor
lead.deck: Thirty-one members in the reeds, fourteen machines, no coughing; a milkman early, a frog unscheduled; Mrs. Grieve not seen, though a woman with a parasol was
lead.body: At ten to five this morning, on the longest day of the year, thirty-one members of the Phonautograph Society crouched in the reeds at Alley Pond with fourteen machines and did not speak. At twenty-five past five the sun came up and so did the birds, forty-seven kinds, Mr. Abbot says. At a quarter past six a Douglaston milk wagon came through early and the driver said good morning to the reeds. He is on the record for 1978. So is a frog.

columns.headline: Party Line's twelfth Friday, and the heat puts her on hold under the counter
columns.body: Twelve Fridays. It was ninety in the parcel room, and Party Line waited for her tin under the counter, flat on the cool linoleum, from four until half past five. No tin came from Corona. Sergeant Moran says the warrant is current. The clerk gave her a saucer of water.

columns.headline: Pun Derby, week three: the undertaker's wife wins on a dead line
columns.body: Week three goes to Mrs. Ida Kranz of Maspeth, whose call to the cemetery could not go through, the line being dead. Five dollars and a year's Speaker. Mr. Kehoe's horse sent 'Neigh' and placed second, the judges being unable to say why. Week four opens Monday.

columns.headline: Feeney won't appeal, and hangs up the wire for the summer
columns.body: Alderman Feeney says he will not appeal Justice Lowry, the Appellate Division going on holiday next Friday anyway. He will spend July on his porch in Astoria with Duke and an electric fan. He says the wire will be heard again. He did not say when.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: No tin for Party Line. The longest day of the year, and she spent the whole of it waiting.

lead.headline: Phonautograph Society records 85 minutes of the dawn at Alley Pond
lead.deck: Fourteen machines from 4:50 a.m.; 47 species identified by ear; Mr. Abbot states the records also carry a tone of 41 cycles 'throughout, beneath the birds'
lead.body: Thirty-one members of the Phonautograph Society of Queens recorded the dawn at Alley Pond yesterday from 4:50 a.m. with 14 machines, Mr. Cyril Abbot states. Forty-seven species were identified by ear. Mr. Abbot states that each record also carries a tone of 41 cycles 'throughout, beneath the birds,' and that the records will be kept for 1978 'as heard.' Queens Light & Power states that Alley Pond is not on its system.

columns.headline: Week's count: 1,174 night calls on the tone in Queens; 801 on the Brooklyn door
columns.body: The Queens Exchange logged 1,174 calls between 1 a.m. and 4 a.m. in the seven nights to Friday reporting a tone, against 1,198, and about 2,000 others concerning neighbours, Superintendent Wilfred Arne states. The Brooklyn Exchange's door shows 801.

columns.headline: Licences: 2,214 granted; 5,210 forms returned; nine days to July 1
columns.body: Mr. Hollis Crane granted 333 licences under the Listening Act in the five days to Friday, 2,214 in all, his office states. Of 6,000 forms, 5,210 have been returned. Licences are required from July 1. The office will open on Saturday and Sunday next.

columns.headline: No parcel for Position 43 on a twelfth Friday; the parcel room at 90 degrees
columns.body: No parcel addressed to 'Party Line, Queens Exchange, Position 43' was received yesterday, the twelfth Friday without one, the supervisor states. The temperature in the parcel room was 90 degrees at 4 p.m. The warrant for Mr. Joseph Marchetti, lineman, remains outstanding.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: WORS 1610 was not heard last night, the forty-fifth night since May 7, the Radio Division states.

speaker.ear: Hot. High 88. Saturday. Nine days to licence your walls.

lead.headline: Landlords queue round Borough Hall, and Mr. Crane's office gets the busy signal
lead.deck: Three hundred and thirty-three licences this week, twenty-two hundred in all; seven hundred and ninety forms still out; one landlord asks for a licence for a parrot
lead.body: Nine days before every listening system in Queens must have a licence, the line outside Mr. Crane's office at Borough Hall went round the corner and back by ten this morning: landlords, churches, two undertakers and the Astoria ferry's purser. Mr. Crane granted three hundred and thirty-three this week. Seven hundred and ninety forms are still out. A Ridgewood landlord applied to licence his parrot, which repeats the tenants. Mr. Crane ruled that a parrot is not a building. The landlord says Mr. Crane has not met the parrot.

columns.headline: Birds go on the record for 1978, and something hums along underneath
columns.body: Mr. Abbot's society took down eighty-five minutes of dawn at Alley Pond yesterday, forty-seven kinds of bird and a milkman. Mr. Abbot says every record carries the forty-one cycles under the birds. The light company says Alley Pond is not on its system. The birds decline comment.

columns.headline: Week's count: Queens rings in about the neighbours, not the tone
columns.body: Queens rang the Exchange about the night tone eleven hundred and seventy-four times this week, down again, and about two thousand times about the neighbours, up a great deal. Brooklyn's door says eight hundred and one. Mr. Tully says nothing, in a notice.

columns.headline: The Listening Lady: a June wedding on one roof, the guests on the next
columns.body: Darlings, the heat has moved society upstairs. Miss Gerda Hoyt of Sunnyside married Mr. Ray Clancy on her mother's roof this afternoon, the church being ninety-four inside. The guests sat on the next roof. The vows were heard on both. The cake went across on a plank.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Rockaway rings the Exchange: music on the sand at four minutes past eleven. We are sending a man with a towel.

editorial.headline: The lady catcher resigns to take up the tango
editorial.body: Ten days ago this newspaper engaged Mr. Silas Pinkney of the Ironclad Detective Agency, a man who has run down bank robbers in three states, to bring us the woman called Lilith. On Thursday Mr. Pinkney resigned. He has sent us his report, which runs to one line: She dances better than I detect. He has enrolled in a dancing school in Jackson Heights and asks us to forward his mail. We have not engaged another detective, there being, Miss Penrose tells us, no detective in Queens who has not already been asked to dance. This paper will catch Lilith itself. We have a plan. We will not print it, in case she reads the Speaker, which she plainly does.

columns.headline: Queens stops on the stoops, and the ice-cream man waits it out
columns.body: With the mercury at eighty-nine and the borough on its steps, half past ten last night came down Thirty-Sixth Avenue like a cloud over a field. Every third person on the block left off, spoon in the air, for two seconds. The other two went on talking. An ice-cream man says he has learned to give change after.

columns.headline: Has Anyone Seen the Professor? A woman in Elmira thinks he owes her
columns.body: Our inquiry has a report from Elmira, where a Mrs. Lull, who may or may not be one, says that Tobias went west in 1919 with a mesmeric act and her mother's clock. She adds that he always did leave before the end. If he is reading this, Queens would like to hear the last word.

columns.headline: Pun Derby: special class for the Emergence opens, and the Editor sighs
columns.body: Entries for the October class may be left at our counter from Monday. We can already report 'Old One for the road,' 'sea you later,' and, from a lady who ought to know better and has lost to us every week since we opened, a thing about a tentacle we cannot print. It is ahead.

columns.headline: Wanted: seat, roof or window, for the night of 12 October
columns.body: Family of five, quiet, own chairs, will pay for a clear view south by west from any roof in Long Island City. References from our present landlord, who would like us to go. Box 412, the Speaker.

back.foot: The Loud Speaker. If it happened, we heard it.

lead.headline: WORS 1610 heard at Rockaway Beach at 11:04 p.m., its first since May 7
lead.deck: About 300 bathers on the sand at Beach 98th Street; heard from the bathing pavilion's loudspeakers, the pavilion's system switched off at 10 p.m., the manager states; shore stations log 12 minutes
lead.body: WORS 1610 was heard at Rockaway Beach at 11:04 p.m. yesterday for the first time since May 7, ending a silence of 45 nights, the Radio Division states. Its shore stations logged 12 minutes of figures. About 300 persons on the sand near Beach 98th Street heard the transmission from the loudspeakers of the Seaside Bathing Pavilion, whose system had been switched off at its board at 10 p.m., the manager, Mr. Carl Brodsky, states. Mr. Harold Pike states that the Division 'notes the place.'

columns.headline: Hottest day of the year: 92 at 2:50 p.m.; 600,000 at Rockaway and Coney
columns.body: The temperature reached 92 degrees at 2:50 p.m. yesterday, the highest of the year, the Weather Bureau states. About 600,000 persons visited Rockaway Beach and Coney Island together. Two persons were overcome in Queens. The school playgrounds remained open overnight.

columns.headline: Exchange logs 388 inquiries on WORS 1610 between 11:05 p.m. and 1 a.m.
columns.body: The Queens Exchange logged 388 inquiries concerning WORS 1610 between 11:05 p.m. and 1 a.m., Superintendent Wilfred Arne states, 112 of them from Rockaway. The Brooklyn Exchange states that it received 'a number' and will post it on the door.

columns.headline: Atlas Casualty Co. to hear Mrs. Dorr's claim on July 9; Mr. Pruett applies
columns.body: The Atlas Casualty Co. states that it will hear the claim of Mrs. Agnes Dorr for the kitchen fire of March 9 at Whitney Avenue, Elmhurst, on July 9. Mr. Gideon Pruett has applied to Mr. Hollis Crane's office for a licence for his house system.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: Mr. Pike's shore stations will sit at Rockaway Beach tonight from 10:30 p.m., the Radio Division states.

speaker.ear: Hot. High 92. Sunday. WORS went swimming.

lead.headline: WORS goes to the beach, and three hundred bathers get perfect reception
lead.deck: Forty-five nights of dead air end at four past eleven on the Rockaway sand; the pavilion's loudspeakers read figures with the board switched off; Mr. Pike notes the place
lead.body: For forty-five nights WORS kept off sixteen-ten, and last night at four minutes past eleven it turned up at Rockaway Beach, in its bathing costume. Three hundred people were on the sand by Beach 98th Street, cooling off, when the loudspeakers of the Seaside Bathing Pavilion began reading figures in a level voice for twelve minutes. Mr. Brodsky, the manager, had switched the pavilion's system off at ten. He showed our man the switch. It was off. Mr. Pike says he notes the place.

columns.headline: Where's WORS? Pin ninety-eight goes in at Rockaway, and the rust can wait
columns.body: Forty-five nights of dead air are over. Our office boy has pulled pin ninety-seven out of the river and put pin ninety-eight in the sand at Beach 98th Street, which he says is a sign. It is a street number. He is twelve.

columns.headline: Ninety-two, and Queens heads for the water at full volume
columns.body: Ninety-two in the shade at ten to three, the year's hottest, and six hundred thousand people went to Rockaway and Coney to stand in the sea. Two were overcome in Queens. The rest were merely overcome by each other, in bathing costumes.

columns.headline: Ask the Operator: 'Can I ring WORS?'
columns.body: Sir, no. The operator has tried every Sunday since November, and WORS is not on the exchange, nor in the book. Three hundred people have gone back to Rockaway tonight to wait for it with sandwiches. Try the sea. It is closer than WORS.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Rockaway at eleven tonight: four hundred on the sand, Mr. Pike's men, our man, the tide. No figures. The tide came in.

lead.headline: Mr. Ruth hits his fifteenth and sixteenth home runs; the Athletics lead by nine
lead.deck: Yankees take three of four from Boston at the Stadium, 61,000 present on Sunday; the Bronx Exchange logs Saturday's home run as 'a report'; Brooklyn loses twice
lead.body: Mr. Babe Ruth hit his fifteenth and sixteenth home runs of the season at the Stadium on Saturday and yesterday as the Yankees won three of four from Boston, the crowd yesterday being estimated at 61,000. The Athletics won twice at Washington and lead the American League by nine games. Mr. Miller Huggins stated that 'the season is long.' The Bronx Exchange logged 41 calls at 3:22 p.m. on Saturday reporting 'a report,' the time of the fifteenth. Brooklyn lost twice to Philadelphia.

columns.headline: Radio Division's shore stations at Rockaway hear nothing on Sunday night
columns.body: Mr. Harold Pike's shore stations sat at Rockaway Beach from 10:30 p.m. to midnight on Sunday and heard nothing on 1610, the Radio Division states. About 400 persons attended on the sand. The Seaside Bathing Pavilion's system had been disconnected at the street.

columns.headline: Licence office to open next Saturday and Sunday; 790 forms outstanding
columns.body: Mr. Hollis Crane's office at Borough Hall will open from 9 a.m. to 6 p.m. on Saturday and Sunday next, licences being required from July 1, his office states. About 790 forms remain outstanding. Mr. Gideon Pruett's application was received on Friday.

columns.headline: Valves at 80 cents the six; Hollander long-life grade sold at 15 cents
columns.body: Valves were quoted at 80 cents the six at Jamaica and Long Island City on Saturday, the Queens Retail Grocers' Association states. The receiver sold the 3,000 long-life valves of the Hollander stock at 15 cents each. Eggs were 38 cents the dozen.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: WORS 1610 was not heard last night, the Radio Division states, its shore stations sitting at Rockaway.

speaker.ear: Hot. High 90. Monday. The landlord rang. Then he ran.

lead.headline: Signal Ground Rents makes its first call, and the caller hangs up at a run
lead.deck: A boy of twelve in a cap leaves a typed demand on ten counters in ninety seconds and is gone up Jackson Avenue; every demand is stamped; Mr. Raab gives chase as far as the elevated
lead.body: At twenty to ten this morning a boy of about twelve in a flat cap came into the Vantry Arcade at a run, put a typed sheet on each of ten counters and ran out again in ninety seconds. Each demands the June rent, four hundred and twelve dollars, and July's on the first, payable at the company's post box. Each is stamped 'by its Secretary.' Mr. Raab chased him up Jackson Avenue to the elevated, where the boy went up the stairs and Mr. Raab did not.

columns.headline: The Babe connects twice, and the Bronx rings in to report the reception
columns.body: The Babe hit his fifteenth on Saturday and his sixteenth yesterday, and forty-one people in the Bronx rang the Exchange at twenty-two past three on Saturday to report a bang. Philadelphia is nine clear anyway. Mr. Huggins says the season is long. So is the gap.

columns.headline: Where's WORS? Four hundred on the sand, and the beach gets dead air
columns.body: Last night four hundred people went back to Rockaway to hear WORS again, and Mr. Pike's men sat with them till midnight. Nothing. Mr. Brodsky has had the pavilion cut off at the street. The tide came in at a quarter to twelve. It was the only thing that did.

columns.headline: Ask the Operator: 'Should I pay the boy?'
columns.body: Sir, if you are in the Arcade, the boy did not stop long enough to be paid, and your rent is with the court clerk anyway. If a boy brings you a demand anywhere else and runs, do not run after him. Mr. Raab tried. Mr. Raab is fifty-three.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Mr. Ewald has taken the ten demands to the Municipal Court clerk, who says the June rent is waiting and always was.

record.ear: Hot, humid. High 94. Low 75. Thunderstorms likely by evening.

lead.headline: Signal Ground Rents serves a demand for the Arcade's rent by messenger
lead.deck: Ten typed demands delivered at 9:40 a.m. by a boy of about twelve, who left at a run; June and July rent demanded, payable at the company's post box; executed by rubber stamp
lead.body: Signal Ground Rents Inc. served its first demand for rent on the ten tenants of the Vantry Arcade at 9:40 a.m. yesterday, a boy of about twelve leaving one on each counter and departing at a run, Mr. Oscar Bliss states. The demands claim the June rent of 412 dollars and the July rent on July 1, 'payable at the Company's box.' Each is executed by the rubber stamp used on the deed. Mr. Nathan Ewald delivered them to the Municipal Court clerk.

columns.headline: Court clerk writes to the company's box that the June rent is held for it
columns.body: Mr. Walter Ingersoll, clerk of the Municipal Court at Long Island City, states that he wrote yesterday to the post office box of Signal Ground Rents Inc. that 412 dollars of June rent 'is held to the Company's credit, and may be called for in person.'

columns.headline: Process server finds the company's box 'not rented' a sixth time
columns.body: Mr. Raab, process server, tried the post office box of Signal Ground Rents Inc. a sixth time yesterday at 3 p.m., with a summons for costs, and found it 'not rented,' the post office states. The clerk's letter was accepted for the box at 4:15 p.m.

columns.headline: Graf Zeppelin's first passenger list for the world flight published
columns.body: The Zeppelin company published at Friedrichshafen yesterday the first list of passengers for the Graf Zeppelin's flight round the world in August, the Berlin wire states. It includes Lady Grace Drummond-Hay, Mr. Karl von Wiegand, Sir Hubert Wilkins and Lieutenant Commander Charles Rosendahl of the Navy.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: WORS 1610 was not heard last night, the Radio Division states.

speaker.ear: Hot. High 94. Tuesday. Thunder after supper, says the Bureau. Bring the cat in.

lead.headline: Zeppelin reads its passenger list down the wire, and everyone wants the line
lead.deck: A lady correspondent, a newspaperman, a polar explorer and a Navy man so far; a fare nobody in Queens can say aloud; Lakehurst to listen her round
lead.body: The Zeppelin people at Friedrichshafen read out their first list of passengers for the August flight round the world this morning, and Berlin sent it down the wire. Lady Grace Drummond-Hay goes, and so does Mr. Karl von Wiegand, both writing for the papers. Sir Hubert Wilkins goes, being an explorer and unable to stop. Commander Rosendahl goes for the Navy. The fare is several thousand dollars. Our office boy has applied, enclosing eleven cents and a sandwich. He has not heard back.

columns.headline: Clerk writes to a box that isn't rented, and the post office puts him through
columns.body: The court clerk wrote to Signal Ground Rents' post box yesterday to say the June rent is waiting. At three Mr. Raab tried the same box and was told it is not rented. At a quarter past four the post office took the clerk's letter for it anyway.

columns.headline: Ninety-four, and the Bureau forecasts a crash on the line by nightfall
columns.body: Ninety-four at three and wet enough to wring, and the Bureau says thunder by evening. The ice men ran out at Woodside by noon. Duchess went home at two in her hat, refusing further duty. A Sunnyside woman has been sitting in her icebox since lunch.

columns.headline: Pun Derby: the receiver picks up the early lead in week four
columns.body: Leading week four: Mr. Saul Feld, grocer, of Jamaica. 'Hollander went bust, so they called in a receiver. Somebody had to pick up.' Mr. Kehoe's horse has entered 'Whoa, please hold.' The judges admit they are softening.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Thunder at Jamaica at a quarter to ten, and the house machines went dark with the lights. Our man is feeling his way along Sutphin Boulevard.

lead.headline: Lightning silences the house systems of Jamaica from 9:52 p.m. to 6:10 a.m.
lead.deck: Signal feeder at the Jamaica junction struck in a storm of 40 minutes; lights out until 1:15 a.m.; temperature falls 19 degrees; no record of the night made in about 8,000 buildings
lead.body: Lightning struck the signal feeder at the Jamaica junction at 9:52 p.m. yesterday during a thunderstorm of about 40 minutes, silencing the house systems of about 8,000 buildings in Jamaica until 6:10 a.m., the Jamaica Signal Exchange states. Light failed in the same district until 1:15 a.m., Queens Light & Power states. The temperature fell 19 degrees in 40 minutes. No record of the night was made in the district. The feeder had not failed 'since 1904,' the Exchange states.

columns.headline: Dr. Rastin to measure the tone from a boat on Jamaica Bay on July 13
columns.body: Dr. Emil Rastin will measure the tone from a rowboat on Jamaica Bay on the night of July 13 at nine stations from Broad Channel, his office states, Mr. Pat Mulry of College Point at the oars. His meter on 31st Street read 41 cycles throughout the storm.

columns.headline: Jamaica precinct reports a quiet night: two arrests, both before the storm
columns.body: The 103rd precinct at Jamaica reports two arrests between 6 p.m. and 6 a.m., both before 9:52 p.m., and no calls after it, the telephones of the district having failed with the house systems. Patrolmen report 'many persons on the stoops.'

columns.headline: Board of Health closes the overnight playgrounds; storms end the heat
columns.body: The Board of Health closed the 14 school playgrounds used as sleeping grounds at 11 p.m. yesterday, the storm having lowered the temperature to 71 degrees. Three persons were struck by falling branches in Queens. None was seriously hurt.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: WORS 1610 was not heard last night, the Radio Division states.

speaker.ear: Cooler. High 76. Wednesday. Jamaica had a night off the record.

lead.headline: Jamaica gets cut off, and the neighbours find they're still on speaking terms
lead.deck: Lightning takes the signal feeder at eight minutes to ten; no machines, no lights, no telephones; eight thousand houses talk on the stoops until the small hours, and nobody takes it down
lead.body: Last night lightning hit the Jamaica signal feeder and every house machine in Jamaica stopped at eight minutes to ten, and the lights with it. For eight hours nothing in Jamaica recorded anything. So Jamaica sat out on its stoops in the cool and talked. Our man walked Sutphin Boulevard with a box of matches and heard a widow tell her neighbour what she really thought of her late husband, a boy propose, and two brothers make up after six years. Nobody wrote it down. Nobody wanted to.

columns.headline: Rastin and Mulry book Jamaica Bay, and the Hum gets another sounding
columns.body: Dr. Rastin will take his meter onto Jamaica Bay on the thirteenth of July, from Broad Channel. Mr. Mulry rows again, at a dollar and a half, the bay being larger. The meter on 31st Street read forty-one all through last night's storm. Lightning did not move it.

columns.headline: Ask the Operator: 'Where was everybody in Jamaica last night?'
columns.body: Madam, on the stoops. The telephones went with the machines at eight minutes to ten, and the operator sat at a board with nobody on it until six. She says it was the first quiet night of her career. She did not care for it.

columns.headline: The Listening Lady: Jamaica, with the machines switched off
columns.body: Darlings, the Listening Lady has nothing from Jamaica, and Jamaica would like it kept that way. She hears there was a proposal on 160th Street, accepted. She hears something was said on Merrick Road that will not be repeated. She did not hear it. Nobody did.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Jamaica came back on at ten past six. Three households have asked the Signal Exchange if they may stay off a while longer.

lead.headline: Ice cream unobtainable at most Queens soda fountains by 2 p.m.; cream short
lead.deck: Long Island Creamery and Meyerhoff Dairy state cream deliveries down a third after the storm; ice at 55 cents; 212 of about 340 fountains report none by mid-afternoon
lead.body: Ice cream could not be had at 212 of about 340 soda fountains and confectioners in Queens by 2 p.m. yesterday, the Queens Retail Druggists' Association states. The Long Island Creamery and the Meyerhoff Dairy state that cream deliveries are down a third, Tuesday's storm having stopped the Jamaica railroad sidings for six hours, and that ice remains short at 55 cents the hundredweight. Meyerhoff will deliver to fountains 'in proportion to last June.' A dish was unchanged at ten cents where served.

columns.headline: Jamaica's house systems resume; no record of Tuesday night exists
columns.body: The Jamaica Signal Exchange states that the house systems of the district resumed at 6:10 a.m. yesterday and that no record of the night of Tuesday exists in any building. Three subscribers have asked that their systems remain disconnected 'for the present.'

columns.headline: Appellate Division rises tomorrow for the summer; 61 appeals undecided
columns.body: The Appellate Division will rise tomorrow until September 23 with 61 appeals undecided, among them Mr. Francis Gorman's appeal against the seal on 11 seconds of the Board of Elections' Riverhead record, the clerk states. Mr. Gorman will attend.

columns.headline: Light company begins printing July bills with the 'Commission credit'
columns.body: Queens Light & Power began printing the July bills for Astoria and Steinway yesterday, each showing a line reading 'Commission credit' for the half cent collected since May 1, the company states. The bills will be delivered from July 3.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: WORS 1610 was not heard last night, the Radio Division states.

speaker.ear: Hot. High 89. Thursday. No ice cream. Don't ask the druggist.

lead.headline: Queens rings every fountain for ice cream, and gets a cold reception
lead.deck: Two hundred and twelve fountains dry by two o'clock; the creameries a third short since the storm; a Flushing druggist sells the last dish at auction for forty cents
lead.body: By two this afternoon two hundred and twelve soda fountains in Queens had no ice cream, and the rest had a queue. The creameries say the cream is a third short since Tuesday's storm stopped the trains at Jamaica, and the ice men are short anyway. In Flushing a druggist auctioned the last dish of vanilla on his counter and got forty cents for it, from a boy who had saved all June. The boy ate it in front of the losers, slowly. Meyerhoff promises more on Friday.

columns.headline: Jamaica comes back on, and three houses ask to stay off the line
columns.body: Jamaica's machines came back at ten past six yesterday morning, and Jamaica is on the record again, mostly. Three households have asked the Signal Exchange to leave them disconnected. The Exchange says they are the first to ask since 1904. It is considering the request.

columns.headline: Gorman's court goes off the air tomorrow, eleven seconds still unheard
columns.body: The Appellate Division rises tomorrow until the twenty-third of September, with Mr. Gorman's eleven seconds still undecided, and sixty other cases. Mr. Gorman will attend the last sitting, his thirty-sixth. He has bought a new hat for it, with the September date already inside.

columns.headline: Pun Derby: the grocer's receiver still leads, and the valves warm up
columns.body: Mr. Feld of Jamaica still leads week four, the bankrupt valve man's receiver having had to pick up. A Corona woman offers: 'My valves and I have a lot in common. We both warm up slowly and blow at the worst moment.' Judging Friday.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: The boy who won the last vanilla in Flushing has been offered sixty cents for the spoon. He is holding out.

lead.headline: Listening Act licences required from Monday; licence office open all weekend
lead.deck: 2,590 granted; 5,600 of 6,000 forms returned; inspection to begin Tuesday in Elmhurst and Astoria; unlicensed systems liable to be disconnected under section 9
lead.body: Licences under the Listening Act will be required for all building listening systems in the State from Monday, July 1, and Mr. Hollis Crane's office at Borough Hall will remain open tomorrow and Sunday, his office states. In Queens 2,590 licences have been granted and 5,600 of 6,000 forms returned. Inspection will begin on Tuesday in Elmhurst and Astoria. Systems found unlicensed may be disconnected under section 9. Mr. Gideon Pruett's licence was granted yesterday.

columns.headline: Fountains limit ice cream to one dish a customer; Meyerhoff deliveries resume
columns.body: The Queens Retail Druggists' Association has asked its members to serve ice cream at one dish a customer until Monday. The Meyerhoff Dairy resumed full deliveries to 140 fountains yesterday afternoon. About 90 fountains reported none by 3 p.m.

columns.headline: Appellate Division rises today; Mr. Gorman to attend his thirty-sixth sitting
columns.body: The Appellate Division sits for the last time before the summer at 10 a.m. today, the clerk states. Mr. Francis Gorman will attend his thirty-sixth sitting. No decision on the seal on 11 seconds of the Riverhead record is expected before September.

columns.headline: Dr. Strand to sail Wednesday; Union Seminary chapel closed for July
columns.body: Dr. Matthias Strand will sail for Liverpool on the Cedric at noon on Wednesday, the seminary states. The Union Seminary chapel will be closed for repairs to its house system during July. The seminary states that the two matters are unconnected.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: WORS 1610 was not heard last night, the Radio Division states.

speaker.ear: Hot. High 91. Friday. Thirteen Fridays. Week four of the Derby.

lead.headline: Pun Derby, week four: the receiver picks up, and the horse is put on hold
lead.deck: Eight thousand cards in four weeks; Mr. Saul Feld of Jamaica takes the five dollars; the horse places second for the third time and engages counsel; the best of the rest, for the record
lead.body: Eight thousand postcards, and the night desk is hoarse. This week's winner is Mr. Saul Feld, grocer, of Jamaica: when Hollander went bust they called in a receiver, because somebody had to pick up. Five dollars and a year's Speaker. Runners-up: the Corona valves that warm up slowly and blow at the worst moment, and a Ridgewood girl who left her husband because he kept putting her on hold. Mr. Kehoe's horse, 'Whoa, please hold,' placed second for the third week. Mr. Kehoe has engaged counsel.

columns.headline: Party Line's thirteenth Friday, and she rings off early
columns.body: Thirteen Fridays. Party Line came to the parcel window at four as usual, waited until a quarter to five and then, for the first time, left early, by the cable door. No tin from Corona. Sergeant Moran says the warrant is current. The clerk says she seemed to know something.

columns.headline: Gorman's court signs off for the summer, eleven seconds unheard
columns.body: The Appellate Division rose at noon today until September. Mr. Gorman sat through the last sitting, his thirty-sixth, and at the end asked the clerk to reserve his seat. The clerk said seats are not reserved. Mr. Gorman left his sandwich on it.

columns.headline: Fountains ration ice cream to a dish, and Queens waits its turn on the line
columns.body: The druggists have ruled one dish a customer until Monday, and Meyerhoff is delivering again, so Queens has ice cream back, a little. In Woodside a man queued twice in a false moustache. He was recognised by the soda jerk, who wore the same one last summer.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Party Line left by the cable door at a quarter to five. The clerk followed her as far as the yard. Then the clerk came back.

lead.headline: Man in a grey coat reads the Arcade rent receipt at the court clerk's window
lead.deck: At 3:40 p.m. yesterday; reads the receipt for 412 dollars through, says 'Correct,' and leaves without the money; the clerk did not ask his name; Mr. Raab at Elmhurst
lead.body: A man of about fifty in a grey coat came to the window of the clerk of the Municipal Court at Long Island City at 3:40 p.m. yesterday and asked to see the receipt for the June rent of the Vantry Arcade, the clerk, Mr. Walter Ingersoll, states. He read the receipt through, said 'Correct,' and left without asking for the 412 dollars. The clerk did not ask his name, 'there being no rule.' Mr. Raab was at Elmhurst. The July rent falls due on Monday.

columns.headline: Week's count: 1,262 night calls on the tone in Queens; 843 on the Brooklyn door
columns.body: The Queens Exchange logged 1,262 calls between 1 a.m. and 4 a.m. in the seven nights to Friday reporting a tone, against 1,174, Superintendent Wilfred Arne states, none from Jamaica on the night of Tuesday. The Brooklyn Exchange's door shows 843.

columns.headline: Licences: 2,702 granted; 5,690 forms returned; office open today and tomorrow
columns.body: Mr. Hollis Crane granted 488 licences under the Listening Act in the five days to Friday, 2,702 in all, his office states. Of 6,000 forms, 5,690 have been returned. The office is open today and tomorrow from 9 a.m. Licences are required from Monday.

columns.headline: No parcel for Position 43 on a thirteenth Friday; the animal leaves early
columns.body: No parcel addressed to 'Party Line, Queens Exchange, Position 43' was received yesterday, the thirteenth Friday without one, the supervisor states. The animal left by the cable door at 4:45 p.m., earlier than usual. The warrant for Mr. Joseph Marchetti, lineman, remains outstanding.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: WORS 1610 was not heard last night, the Radio Division states.

speaker.ear: Fair. High 86. Saturday. The grey coat came back. He still says one word.

lead.headline: The grey coat calls at the court, and leaves the June rent on hold
lead.deck: Twenty to four at the clerk's window, as in May; 'Correct'; four hundred and twelve dollars left sitting; the July rent due Monday, and Mr. Raab was in Elmhurst again
lead.body: At twenty to four yesterday, the hour he took the May rent, the man in the grey coat walked up to the court clerk's window in Long Island City and asked to see the receipt for the Arcade's June rent. He read it through. He said 'Correct.' Then he walked out and left the four hundred and twelve dollars behind. Mr. Raab was in Elmhurst, as he always is. The July rent falls due on Monday, and the Arcade has started a pool on where.

columns.headline: Licence rush: 488 in a week, and Mr. Crane's clerks can't hang up
columns.body: Mr. Crane's office granted four hundred and eighty-eight licences this week, half as many again as last, and opens today and tomorrow. Mr. Pruett has his. The Ridgewood parrot has none. The parrot's landlord says it has stopped talking anyway, out of pride.

columns.headline: Week's count: the tone rings in louder, and Brooklyn's door keeps up
columns.body: The Exchange took twelve hundred and sixty-two calls about the night tone this week, up for the first time since May. Jamaica did not ring on Tuesday night, having no telephones. Brooklyn's door reads eight hundred and forty-three. Mr. Tully has run out of notices.

columns.headline: The Listening Lady: the last June brides, and one groom lost at Rockaway
columns.body: Darlings, June ends with nine weddings today, all recorded, and one groom who went to Rockaway last Saturday to hear WORS and came home on Tuesday sunburnt and engaged to somebody else. The first fiancee has kept the ring and the gramophone.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: The Arcade pool on the July rent: court clerk, two to one; the post box, five to one; the grey coat, evens.

editorial.headline: Operators of the borough form a league
editorial.body: The telephone operators of Queens, the young women who connect every call in this borough because no house in it can dial, have formed a Lilith League and say they will strike unless they are paid for the hours they are held on a line by gentlemen who wish to talk to a pretty voice. This paper has always held that an operator should be heard and not seen. We now learn she can also stop hearing. The company has offered them two cents an hour. They have answered, on every line in the borough at once, with a single word, which we will not print, and which was said very sweetly. The company has offered four.

lead.headline: Mexico City cathedral's bells heard by wire for the first time since 1926
lead.deck: Settlement between the Mexican Government and the bishops of June 21 permits public worship from today; the bells carried for eleven minutes at noon; played in this newspaper's window at 1:10 p.m.
lead.body: The bells of the cathedral of Mexico City were rung at noon yesterday for the first time since public worship was suspended in July 1926, the Mexico wire states, following the settlement between the Government of President Portes Gil and the bishops announced on June 21. Public worship resumes today. The wire carried the bells for eleven minutes. They were played in this newspaper's window on Jackson Avenue at 1:10 p.m. to about 300 persons, some of whom knelt on the pavement.

columns.headline: Mr. Ruth's eighteenth home run; the Yankees end June nine games behind
columns.body: Mr. Babe Ruth hit his seventeenth and eighteenth home runs of the season at Philadelphia yesterday, the Yankees winning 8 to 4 but ending June nine games behind the Athletics, who lead the American League. Brooklyn beat Boston at Ebbets Field.

columns.headline: Listening Act licences required from tomorrow; office open until 6 p.m. today
columns.body: Licences under the Listening Act are required from tomorrow. Mr. Hollis Crane's office at Borough Hall granted 140 licences yesterday, 2,842 in all, and will remain open until 6 p.m. today. Inspection begins on Tuesday in Elmhurst and Astoria.

columns.headline: WORS 1610 not heard since Rockaway; shore stations to sit there through July
columns.body: WORS 1610 has not been heard since 11:16 p.m. on June 22 at Rockaway Beach, the Radio Division states. Mr. Harold Pike's shore stations will sit at Rockaway from 10:30 p.m. nightly through July. The Seaside Bathing Pavilion remains disconnected at the street.

record.wire: LATE WIRE: Mr. Nathan Ewald advises the ten Arcade tenants to deposit the July rent with the clerk of the Municipal Court at 10 a.m. tomorrow.

speaker.ear: Fair. High 82. Sunday. June's over. Licence your walls by midnight.

lead.headline: Mexico gives the church a ring after three years, and Jackson Avenue picks up
lead.deck: Eleven minutes of the cathedral's bells by the Mexico wire, played in the Record's window; three hundred stop, some kneel; a trolley stops too, the motorman taking off his cap
lead.body: At ten past one yesterday the Record played the bells of Mexico City's cathedral in its window on Jackson Avenue, eleven minutes of them, rung at noon for the first time in three years. We do not often praise the Record. Three hundred people stopped on the pavement. Some knelt, in the heat, on the stone. A trolley stopped too, and the motorman took his cap off and held it until the last bell. It was a fine sound.

columns.headline: The Babe signs off June with eighteen, and Philadelphia stays nine ahead
columns.body: The Babe hit two at Philadelphia yesterday, his seventeenth and eighteenth, and the Yankees won, and the Athletics are still nine games clear at the end of June. Mr. Huggins says July is long. Mr. Ruth says he will hit more. He usually does.

columns.headline: Where's WORS? Seven nights since the beach, and Pike's men take deck chairs
columns.body: Seven nights since WORS read its figures at Rockaway, and nothing since. Mr. Pike's shore men will sit on the beach every night in July, which their wives call a holiday and they call duty. Our office boy's pin ninety-eight is still in the sand.

columns.headline: Ask the Operator: 'Do I need a licence for my walls?'
columns.body: Sir, from midnight, if your walls listen. Ordinary walls need nothing. Walls with a machine in them need Mr. Crane's licence, and he is open until six today. If you are not sure which walls you have, say something unkind about your landlord, and wait.

speaker.wire: LATE WIRE: Mr. Crane closed his door at six and granted his last licence of June to a Flushing church. It had been waiting since April.
